Abstract:
Gesture recognition presents a promising avenue for interfacing with unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) due to its intuitive nature and potential for precise interaction. This research conducts a comprehensive comparative analysis of vision-based hand gesture detection methodologies tailored for UAV Control. The existing gesture recognition approaches involving cropping, zooming, and color-based segmentation, do not work well for this kind of applications in dynamic conditions and suffer in performance with increasing distance and environmental noises. We propose to use a novel approach leveraging hand landmarks drawing and classification for gesture recognition based UAV control. With experimental results we show that our proposed method outperforms the other existing methods in terms of accuracy, noise resilience, and efficacy across varying distances, thus providing robust control decisions. However, implementing the deep learning based compute intensive gesture recognition algorithms on the UAV's onboard computer is significantly challenging in terms of performance. Hence, we propose to use a edge-computing based framework to offload the heavier computing tasks, thus achieving closed-loop real-time performance. With implementation over AirSim simulator as well as over a real-world UAV, we showcase the advantage of our end-to-end gesture recognition based UAV control system.

Abstract:
This paper presents the design and implementation of an AI vision-controlled orthotic hand exoskeleton to enhance rehabilitation and assistive functionality for individuals with hand mobility impairments. The system leverages a Google Coral Dev Board Micro with an Edge TPU to enable real-time object detection using a customized MobileNet\_V2 model trained on a six-class dataset. The exoskeleton autonomously detects objects, estimates proximity, and triggers pneumatic actuation for grasp-and-release tasks, eliminating the need for user-specific calibration needed in traditional EMG-based systems. The design prioritizes compactness, featuring an internal battery. It achieves an 8-hour runtime with a 1300 mAh battery. Experimental results demonstrate a 51ms inference speed, a significant improvement over prior iterations, though challenges persist in model robustness under varying lighting conditions and object orientations. While the most recent YOLO model (YOLOv11) showed potential with 15.4 FPS performance, quantization issues hindered deployment. The prototype underscores the viability of vision-controlled exoskeletons for real-world assistive applications, balancing portability, efficiency, and real-time responsiveness, while highlighting future directions for model optimization and hardware miniaturization.

Abstract:
Realization of situation-awareness for autonomous robotics applications in edge computing environment is challenging. First, computing capabilities of edge devices are limited, which must be considered in the execution of machine learning (ML)-based solutions. Second, many technologies are available for realizing situation-aware capabilities, but comparison and integration of solutions creates additional challenges. Third, existing ML-based models are often not directly applicable for realizing custom applications, and model(s) may need to be re-trained with new data. The contribution of this paper is efficiency and feasibility evaluation of human pose recognition and object detection technologies in edge computing environment. Several lessons learnt covering constraints are presented regarding feasibility of the experimented technologies and data sets. The efficiency evaluation results indicated that simultaneous human pose recognition (Google’s Movenet) and object detection (Yolov5) on Jetson AGX Xavier achieved ~13-16 FPS, while GPU and CPU utilization remained at a medium level, and most of the memory remained unused (< 44 %). Object concept and human pose concept activation algorithms may be considered as an additional contribution. Realized architecture design of the prototyped system in multiple computing environments can be considered as a partial evaluation of a ML-based big data reference architecture.

Abstract:
Choosing the appropriate deployment strategy for any Deep Learning (DL) project in a production environment has always been the most challenging problem for industrial practitioners. There are several conflicting constraints and controversial approaches when it comes to deployment. Among these problems, the deployment on cloud versus the deployment on edge represents a common dilemma. In a nutshell, each approach provides benefits where the other would have limitations. This paper presents a real-world case study on deploying a face recognition application using MTCNN detector and FaceNet recognizer. We report the challenges faced to decide on the best deployment strategy. We propose three inference architectures for the deployment, including cloud-based, edge-based, and hybrid. Furthermore, we evaluate the performance of face recognition inference on different cloud-based and edge-based GPU platforms. We consider different models of Jetson boards for the edge (Nano, TX2, Xavier NX, Xavier AGX) and various GPUs for the cloud (GTX 1080, RTX 2080Ti, RTX 2070, and RTX 8000). We also investigate the effect of deep learning model optimization using TensorRT and TFLite compared to a standard Tensorflow GPU model, and the effect of input resolution. We provide a benchmarking study for all these devices in terms of frames per second, execution times, energy and memory usages. After conducting a total of 294 experiments, the results demonstrate that the TensorRT optimization provides the fastest execution on all cloud and edge devices, at the expense of significantly larger energy consumption (up to +40% and +35% for edge and cloud devices, respectively, compared to Tensorflow). Whereas TFLite is the most efficient framework in terms of memory and power consumption, while providing significantly less (-4% to -62%) processing acceleration than TensorRT.     author = "Hwang, Guebin and Lee, Taeyeop and Lee, Y. and Shin, Hyosup and Jo, Sungho",

    year = "2026",

Relevant Snippet:
Recent robot systems combine wrist and fixed cameras, requiring camera-to-robot transforms for both. Most hand-eye calibration methods rely on targets or robot-body observations. Scene-based methods using 3D reconstruction require neither but address only wrist cameras. We introduce AnchorHEC, a targetless hand-eye calibration framework for wrist and fixed cameras in a single procedure using RGB images, forward kinematics (FK), and known camera intrinsics. We initialize both camera types using FK and a shared 3D foundation model reconstruction. FK-constrained wrist-image bundle adjustment reduces the impact of reconstructed pose and scale errors. If this refinement fails or retains too few inliers, we relax the constraints on potentially inaccurate FK poses and lens parameters. We use the refined wrist transform and FK to triangulate metric points and estimate fixed-camera poses. Across three backbones, calibration errors in simulation decrease by 86.4% in translation and 71.6% in rotation, averaged over both camera types, relative to reconstruction-based baselines. We also validate AnchorHEC on a physical robot. Project page: https://hwanggb.github.io/AnchorHEC/

Abstract:
Ensuring robot safety can be challenging; user-defined constraints can miss edge cases, policies can become unsafe even when trained from safe data, and safety can be subjective. Thus, we learn about robot safety by showing policy trajectories to a human who flags unsafe behavior. From this binary feedback, we use the statistical method of conformal prediction to identify a region of states, potentially in learned latent space, guaranteed to contain a user-specified fraction of future policy errors. Our method is sample-efficient, as it builds on nearest neighbor classification and avoids withholding data as is common with conformal prediction. By alerting if the robot reaches the suspected unsafe region, we obtain a warning system that mimics the human's safety preferences with guaranteed miss rate. From video labeling, our system can detect when a quadcopter visuomotor policy will fail to steer through a designated gate. We present an approach for policy improvement by avoiding the suspected unsafe region. With it we improve a model predictive controller's safety, as shown in experimental testing with 30 quadcopter flights across 6 navigation tasks. Code and videos are provided.

Abstract:
When deploying machine learning models in high-stakes robotics applications, the ability to detect unsafe situations is crucial. Early warning systems can provide alerts when an unsafe situation is imminent (in the absence of corrective action). To reliably improve safety, these warning systems should have a provable false negative rate; that is, of the situations that are unsafe, fewer than ϵ will occur without an alert. In this work, we present a framework that combines a statistical inference technique known as conformal prediction with a simulator of robot/environment dynamics, in order to tune warning systems to provably achieve an ϵ false negative rate using as few as 1/ϵ data points. We apply our framework to a driver warning system and a robotic grasping application, and empirically demonstrate the guaranteed false negative rate while also observing a low false detection (positive) rate.

Abstract:
We consider perception-based control using state estimates that are obtained from high-dimensional sensor measurements via learning-enabled perception maps. However, these perception maps are not perfect and result in state estimation errors that can lead to unsafe system behavior. Stochastic sensor noise can make matters worse and result in estimation errors that follow unknown distributions. We propose a perception-based control framework that i) quantifies estimation uncertainty of perception maps, and ii) integrates these uncertainty representations into the control design. To do so, we use conformal prediction to compute valid state estimation regions, which are sets that contain the unknown state with high probability. We then devise a sampled-data controller for continuous-time systems based on the notion of measurement robust control barrier functions. Our controller uses idea from self-triggered control and enables us to avoid using stochastic calculus. Our framework is agnostic to the choice of the perception map, independent of the noise distribution, and to the best of our knowledge the first to provide probabilistic safety guarantees in such a setting. Abstract:
We propose a framework for planning in unknown dynamic environments with probabilistic safety guarantees using conformal prediction. Particularly, we design a model predictive controller (MPC) that uses i) trajectory predictions of the dynamic environment, and ii) prediction regions quantifying the uncertainty of the predictions. To obtain prediction regions, we use conformal prediction, a statistical tool for uncertainty quantification, that requires availability of offline trajectory data – a reasonable assumption in many applications such as autonomous driving. The prediction regions are valid, i.e., they hold with a user-defined probability, so that the MPC is provably safe. We illustrate the results in the self-driving car simulator CARLA at a pedestrian-filled intersection. The strength of our approach is compatibility with state of the art trajectory predictors, e.g., RNNs and LSTMs, while making no assumptions on the underlying trajectory-generating distribution. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first results that provide valid safety guarantees in such a setting.

{"answer": "## Vision-Based Verification, Human Detection, Calibration, and Privacy for Cloud Laboratory Automation

### 1. Accuracy of Vision and Vision-Language Success/Failure Detectors

The following table summarizes reported accuracy metrics across the major systems identified in the literature:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**LIRA (Zhou et al. 2025; peer-reviewed).** The most directly relevant system for self-driving laboratories is LIRA, which uses a fine-tuned vision-language model on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin (64 GB) edge computing module. Across 200 manually introduced placement errors in two autonomous laboratory workflows (solid-state and synthesis), the fine-tuned VLM achieved 97.9% overall accuracy for determining whether placement was correct, 96.8% for classifying misalignment direction, and 98.9% for predicting whether an error was recoverable (pqac-00000010). Five failures occurred out of 200 tests (2 PXRD-plate and 3 NMR-rack errors), yielding a 97.5% error-inspection success rate (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008). By comparison, a conventional YOLOv11 classifier reached only 86.3%, and a zero-shot LLaVA-OneVision model achieved 42.9% (pqac-00000010). The system used an Intel RealSense D435i camera on the robot end effector and fixed webcams on instruments (pqac-00000009). DOI: 10.1038/s42004-025-01770-1.

**SuccessVQA / Flamingo (Du et al. 2023; preprint).** Fine-tuned Flamingo-3B evaluated on Panda gear-manipulation tasks achieved in-domain balanced accuracies of 82.1–96.0% for insertion and removal tasks, with approximately 50,000–60,000 episodes evaluated per task and 2,076 held-out episodes (pqac-00000058). Critically, changing the viewpoint from the front basket camera (used for training) to the rear camera reduced balanced accuracy by up to 7.5 percentage points (from 96.0% to 89.7% for large-gear insertion; from 87.2% to 79.4% for large-gear removal) (pqac-00000059). Adding distractor objects caused minimal degradation. This demonstrates that viewpoint is a significant factor even for fine-tuned models. arXiv: 2303.07280.

**Guardian (Pacaud et al. 2025; preprint).** Guardian-8B correctly recognized 91% of successful executions and 76% of failed executions, with a 9% false-positive rate on a UR5/RG6 multi-camera setup (pqac-00000004). On benchmark datasets, it achieved execution accuracy of 0.86 on RoboFail, 0.77 on UR5-Fail, and 0.85 on RoboVQA (pqac-00000003). arXiv: 2512.01946.

**Robometer (Liang et al. 2026; preprint).** On 100 Franka Panda DROID trajectories (30 successes, 70 failures, seven tasks), Robometer achieved a mean F1 of 0.81, outperforming RoboReward-4B (0.74), GPT-5-mini (0.33), and VLAC (0.16) (pqac-00000017). arXiv: 2603.02115.

**Gemini Robotics-ER 1.5 (GR Team 2025; preprint).** The system was evaluated for binary video success detection across real-time (inference at 5 Hz) and offline settings, with both multiview and singleview inputs (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000057). The text emphasizes that stale predictions due to inference latency can render real-time judgments unreliable during dynamic interactions. The specific 82.4% figure mentioned in the user's context could not be confirmed from the retrieved text; Figure 13 of the paper plots values approximately ranging from the high-0.4s to about 0.8 depending on setting and model (pqac-00000006). arXiv: 2510.03342.

**FailBench (Navasardyan et al. 2026; preprint).** This cross-source benchmark evaluated 13 VLM-based detectors across 2,197 manipulation attempts from 14 independent sources (1,176 failures, 1,021 successes; 73% real-world). The strongest detector achieved 0.77 mean balanced accuracy. Critically, "no model exceeds 0.60 balanced accuracy on contact-rich assembly" (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002). Purpose-built failure detectors generally underperformed general-purpose VLMs (pqac-00000005). arXiv: 2609.03611.

**SAFE (Gu et al. 2025; preprint).** SAFE extracts VLA internal features and predicts failure likelihood. On real-world data, SAFE-MLP achieved ROC-AUC of 86.76–89.11 on seen tasks and 88.42 on unseen WidowX tasks (pqac-00000050). It uses functional conformal prediction to calibrate time-varying detection thresholds, with significance level α ≈ 0.15 providing a tradeoff between balanced accuracy and detection latency (pqac-00000055). arXiv: 2506.09937.

**Edge deployment.** Among the systems reviewed, only LIRA demonstrated deployment on edge hardware suitable for a small cloud lab (Jetson AGX Orin) (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000014). Failures were attributed to "visually ambiguous conditions, such as similar rack/holder colors or cluttered backgrounds" (pqac-00000008). DOI: 10.1038/s42004-025-01770-1.

**Fontenot et al. 2026** was not found in the literature search. No publication matching this author and date was retrievable. If it exists, it may be too recent to have been indexed.

**AnchorHEC (Hwang et al. 2026; preprint)** is a targetless hand-eye calibration framework for jointly calibrating wrist and fixed cameras using RGB images, forward kinematics, and known camera intrinsics, without calibration targets. In simulation, AnchorHEC reduced translation calibration error by 86.4% and rotation error by 71.6% compared to reconstruction-based baselines (pqac-00000020). The standard approach in robotics is periodic re-verification against known fiducial markers—which aligns with the user's current AprilTag infrastructure. **Conformal prediction** provides the most principled framework for bounding false-negative rates (missed failures) of vision-based decision gates. Luo et al. (2023; peer-reviewed) demonstrated that conformal prediction can tune warning systems to provably achieve a false-negative rate ≤ ε using as few as 1/ε unsafe calibration examples—approximately 20 examples for a 5% FNR target (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000042). Failures were attributed to "visually ambiguous conditions, such as similar rack/holder colors or cluttered backgrounds" (pqac-00000008). DOI: 10.1038/s42004-025-01770-1.

**Smallest detectable offsets.** No published work was found that specifically quantifies the smallest positional offset (in mm) detectable by a vision system for labware placement verification. LIRA's misalignment classification distinguishes translational offsets (left, right, forward, backward) from rotational errors, treating translational errors as recoverable and rotational errors as requiring human intervention (pqac-00000011), but it does not report minimum detectable displacement thresholds. **This remains a gap in the published literature** relevant to the user's vial-seating and stub-insertion verification needs.

**Fontenot et al. 2026** was not found in the literature search. No publication matching this author and date was retrievable. If it exists, it may be too recent to have been indexed.

---

### 4. Calibration Maintenance and Drift Detection

**AnchorHEC (Hwang et al. 2026; preprint)** is a targetless hand-eye calibration framework for jointly calibrating wrist and fixed cameras using RGB images, forward kinematics, and known camera intrinsics, without calibration targets. In simulation, AnchorHEC reduced translation calibration error by 86.4% and rotation error by 71.6% compared to reconstruction-based baselines (pqac-00000020). On a physical robot, wrist-camera calibration achieved 1.22–1.35 cm translation error and 1.00–1.48° rotation error at 15 wrist poses (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000022). Fixed-camera translation errors averaged approximately 1.29 cm for accepted registrations (pqac-00000022). The method supports recalibration from a single scene acquisition without dedicated targets. arXiv: 2611.02884.

**Self-calibration using contact.** Limoyo et al. (2018; peer-reviewed) demonstrated targetless self-calibration for mobile manipulators using point-cloud registration, achieving centimeter-level accuracy for end-effector positioning under visual guidance. DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.1803.06406.

**Drift detection.** No published work was found that specifically addresses automated detection of extrinsic calibration drift during long campaigns. The standard approach in robotics is periodic re-verification against known fiducial markers—which aligns with the user's current AprilTag infrastructure. A practical self-check would compare the detected tag poses against their known fixture positions at regular intervals; if reprojection error exceeds a threshold, recalibration is triggered. **No published study reports how often recalibration is needed for low-cost cameras like the IMX477**, nor whether the IMX477 exhibits greater thermal or mechanical drift than industrial cameras. This is an open gap.

---

### 5. Measuring and Bounding False-Clear / False-Success Rates for Vision Gates

**Conformal prediction** provides the most principled framework for bounding false-negative rates (missed failures) of vision-based decision gates. Luo et al. (2023; peer-reviewed) demonstrated that conformal prediction can tune warning systems to provably achieve a false-negative rate ≤ ε using as few as 1/ε unsafe calibration examples—approximately 20 examples for a 5% FNR target (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000042). The key tradeoff is that demanding very low FNR imposes a lower bound on false-positive rate: FPR ≥ 1 − (1+T)·ε, where T is the training-set size (pqac-00000037). DOI: 10.1177/02783649231221580.

**PAC-Bayes bounds.** Farid et al. (2022; preprint) achieved misclassification bounds of 0.128 for standard navigation and 0.154 for occluded-obstacle settings using PAC-Bayes analysis of a vision-based failure predictor. In 15 physical trials per setting, no false negatives (collisions) occurred when the predictor was used (pqac-00000038). arXiv: 2202.05894.

**SAFE's functional conformal prediction.** SAFE uses a time-varying conformal prediction band calibrated on successful rollouts, with significance level α (typically 0.15) controlling the accuracy-latency tradeoff. A failure is flagged when the score exceeds the threshold (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000055). This framework is directly applicable to gating decisions like "is the plate clear?"

**Practical implication for the plate-clear check.** No published study reports the false-clear rate of a specific vision gate for 3D-printer plate clearing. To measure this, one would: (a) collect labeled examples of clear and not-clear plates, (b) run the classifier on a held-out set, (c) apply conformal prediction to bound the false-clear (false-negative) rate at a user-specified level (e.g., ε = 0.05), requiring approximately 20 deliberately not-clear images. The conformal guarantee holds marginally under exchangeability; distribution shifts (lighting changes, camera drift) can violate this assumption.

---

### 6. Privacy, Governance, and Anonymization Effects

**Effect of face blurring on downstream detection.** Ren et al. (2018; peer-reviewed) found that Gaussian face blurring reduced spatial action detection mAP on the DALY dataset from 56.85% to 42.39–51.97% depending on blur severity (a 5–14.5 point drop), while masking caused the largest degradation to 38.86% (pqac-00000029). Their adversarially learned anonymizer maintained mAP at 52.32%, outperforming all hand-crafted methods. arXiv: 1803.11556.

Lee & You (2024; peer-reviewed) found that face blurring reduced YOLOv8x bbox mAP by 2.6 points and RT-DETR-L by 7.5 points on COCO, but person-class detection was relatively robust due to the strong representation of persons in training data (pqac-00000034). DOI: 10.1109/ACCESS.2024.3352146.

Abdulaziz & Bondarev (2026; peer-reviewed) showed that for video anomaly detection, blurring caused only minor AUC degradation (0.2–0.5 points for robust models like UR-DMU and PEL4VAD), while masking could paradoxically improve some models but at the cost of extreme false-alarm rates (99.65% for BN-WVAD) (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000035). DOI: 10.1007/978-3-032-07343-3_14.

**Practical guidance for the BYU lab.** At 720p and 5 FPS with on-device face blurring, the user's setup should expect modest degradation (2–8 points mAP) for person and object detection. For hand-entry detection, hands are typically not blurred, so hand-detection accuracy should be unaffected by face anonymization. Activity recognition for face-centric actions (e.g., drinking) would be more impacted, but laboratory manipulations are hand-centric and thus less sensitive.

**Governance.** No published standard specific to laboratory video governance was found. General guidance from GDPR and institutional review board frameworks applies: face de-identification should occur at the point of capture (as the user is already doing), retention policies should be defined and enforced, and access controls should limit who can view raw (un-blurred) footage. The key unresolved question is whether blurred video constitutes personal data under applicable regulations if re-identification is technically possible through de-blurring attacks, as noted in the privacy literature (pqac-00000036).

---

### Summary of Gaps in Published Evidence

Several aspects of the user's question have **no published evidence**:

1. **False-clear rate of a 3D-printer plate check**: No study has measured this specific vision gate's error rate.
2. **Smallest detectable labware offset** (in mm): Not quantified in any retrieved publication.
3. **Calibration drift rates for IMX477 or similar low-cost cameras**: No published data.
4. **How often recalibration is needed** for wrist or fixed cameras during long laboratory campaigns: Not reported.
5. **ISO 13849/IEC 61496 certification of camera-based detection**: No deep-learning camera system has achieved formal safety certification for robot workcell human detection.
6. **Laboratory-specific video retention or governance standards**: None found; general data-protection frameworks apply.
7. **Fontenot et al. 2026**: Not found in the literature search.
8. **quARtet multi-tag fiducials**: Not found in the peer-reviewed robotics or laboratory automation literature."}

Context. We run a small cloud lab at BYU (the Vertical Cloud Lab) with an AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm and Raspberry Pi 5 computers carrying Pi HQ (IMX477) and Camera Module 3 cameras, both fixed around the cell and on the wrist. Today we localize fixtures with AprilTags (25 mm tags read reliably at about 1 m; 10 mm tags did not read at all), no camera is calibrated to the arm yet, and the cell is livestreamed at 720p and 5 frames per second with on-device face blurring. We are starting a ledger of every handling step and every human intervention (for 3D-printer plate clearing, loading vials into a gantry liquid handler, and moving SEM stubs and sealed powder jars), and we want the cameras to do more than localize: verify outcomes (plate clear, vial seated, stub inserted, jar on the balance, powder spilled), detect human interventions and hands entering the cell automatically so the ledger does not depend on people remembering to log, and notice when a camera's calibration has drifted. Our 3D-printing workflow already refuses to start a print until a camera frame shows the plate clear, but nobody has measured how often such a check is wrong. We know of LIRA (Zhou et al. 2025; a fine-tuned vision-language model on an edge box caught 195 of 200 hand-placed errors), Gemini Robotics ER 2 (reported 82.4% video success detection), the Robometer and TOPReward success scorers in LeRobot, multi-tag fiducials such as quARtet, and targetless wrist-plus-fixed camera calibration (AnchorHEC).

Question.
(1) What accuracy have vision and vision-language success or failure detectors achieved on real robot manipulation outcomes, especially laboratory tasks? Report precision, recall and false-success rates with trial counts, how results change with viewpoint, resolution, frame rate and lighting, and which models run on edge hardware such as a Raspberry Pi 5 with or without an accelerator, or a Jetson.
(2) Automatic detection of human interventions and human presence in robot workcells from ordinary cameras (hand or body detection, pose estimation, activity recognition): measured accuracy and latency, use for logging versus for safety, and the status of camera-based safety functions under ISO 13849, IEC 61496 and ISO 10218:2025.
(3) Camera verification of placement and insertion (seated or not, offset estimates) for labware: measured accuracy and the smallest offsets detected, for example in LIRA, Fontenot et al. 2026, or rack-insertion work.
(4) Calibration maintenance: methods to detect extrinsic drift of fixed and wrist cameras during long campaigns (self-checks against fixture tags, targetless methods), how often recalibration was needed, and any results for low-cost cameras such as the IMX477.
(5) How should the false-clear or false-success rate of a vision check that gates the next action (such as starting a print) be measured and bounded, and what rates have been reported for such gates?
(6) Privacy and governance for continuously recorded or livestreamed laboratory video (face blurring, retention), and whether anonymization degrades detection.

Prefer peer-reviewed sources from 2015 to 2026, and flag preprints. For each claim give the DOI or arXiv ID and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.

## Vision-Based Verification, Human Detection, Calibration, and Privacy for Cloud Laboratory Automation

### 1. Accuracy of Vision and Vision-Language Success/Failure Detectors

The following table summarizes reported accuracy metrics across the major systems identified in the literature:

| System | Year | Type | Metric reported | Value | Trials / samples | Hardware / edge capability | Domain | Key limitation |
|---|---:|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|---|
| LIRA | 2025 | Peer-reviewed | Placement-inspection accuracy; direction accuracy; recoverability accuracy | 97.9%; 96.8%; 98.9% | 200 manually introduced placement tests; 195/200 correct in the reported workflow test | NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin 64 GB running the fine-tuned VLM; RealSense D435i | Self-driving laboratory racks and plates: Chemspeed, PXRD, LCMS, NMR | Five misses included two PXRD-plate and three NMR-rack cases; primarily placement verification, not general manipulation; precision, recall, and false-success rate were not reported separately (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 7-8, zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 8-9, zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 5-7) |
| SuccessVQA / fine-tuned Flamingo-3B | 2023 | Preprint | Episode-level balanced accuracy | Front view: 82.1–96.0%; changed rear view: 75.9–91.0%; distractors: 82.4–96.1% | 2,076 held-out episodes; approximately 50,000–60,000 evaluated episodes per task in the in-domain analysis | Flamingo-3B; no Raspberry Pi or Jetson deployment demonstrated | General manipulation: Panda robot inserting/removing three gear sizes | Removal was harder than insertion; changing viewpoint reduced balanced accuracy by as much as 7.5 points; no edge benchmark or precision/recall report (du2023visionlanguagemodelsas pages 9-12, du2023visionlanguagemodelsas pages 12-14) |
| Guardian-8B | 2025 | Preprint | Success/failure accuracy; successful- and failed-execution recognition | 91% of successes and 76% of failures recognized; benchmark execution accuracy 0.77–0.86 | Detector-test count not stated in the retrieved results; separate reasoning analysis used 300 samples | 8B model; no Raspberry Pi/Jetson runtime reported | General real-robot manipulation using UR5/RG6 and multi-camera datasets | Failure recall was substantially below success recall; precision and deployment latency were not reported (pacaud2025guardiandetectingrobotic pages 5-6, pacaud2025guardiandetectingrobotic pages 9-11) |
| Robometer | 2026 | Preprint | Mean F1 for zero-shot failure detection | 0.81 | 100 DROID trajectories: 30 successes, 70 failures, seven tasks | 4B reward model; no constrained-edge benchmark reported | General Franka Panda manipulation | Small test set and class imbalance; subtle towel-folding and tissue-pulling failures remained difficult; no separate precision/recall values (liang2026robometerscalinggeneralpurpose pages 9-10) |
| SAFE-MLP / SAFE-LSTM | 2025 | Preprint | Real-world rollout ROC-AUC; balanced-accuracy/latency trade-off | SAFE-MLP: 86.76–89.11 on seen and 88.42 on unseen WidowX tasks; SAFE-LSTM: 77.27–84.29 seen and 71.80 unseen | Exact rollout count not stated in the retrieved passages | Reads internal OpenVLA, π0, or π0-FAST features; no Raspberry Pi/Jetson deployment reported | Multitask VLA failure detection in simulation and real manipulation | Requires access to policy internals; conformal guarantees may fail under seen-to-unseen distribution shift; retrieved results do not give F1 or exact balanced accuracy (gu2026safemultitaskfailure pages 9-11, gu2026safemultitaskfailure pages 19-21) |
| AHA-13B | 2024 | Preprint | RoboFail execution-failure accuracy | 0.64 | Not stated in the retrieved comparison | 13B VLM; no constrained-edge deployment reported | General manipulation failure detection and explanation | Real-world score reported only through a later comparison; precision, recall, false-success rate, latency, and trial count unavailable (pacaud2025guardiandetectingrobotic pages 5-6) |
| FailBench best detector | 2026 | Preprint | Mean balanced accuracy across independent sources | 0.77; no model exceeded 0.60 on contact-rich assembly | 2,197 attempts from 14 sources: 1,176 failures and 1,021 successes; 12 real and two simulated sources | Benchmark of 13 detectors; hardware deployment not evaluated | Cross-source general manipulation, including policy rollouts, teleoperation, and constructed failures | Performance approached chance when success required judging physical contact; purpose-built detectors often underperformed general-purpose VLMs; no aggregate precision/recall report (navasardyan2026failbenchhowreliable pages 2-4, navasardyan2026failbenchhowreliable pages 4-6, navasardyan2026failbenchhowreliable pages 1-2) |
| Gemini Robotics-ER 1.5 | 2025 | Preprint | Binary video success-detection accuracy in real-time/offline and single-/multiview settings | Figure-level values approximately high-0.4 to about 0.8; the claimed 82.4% and its denominator were not recoverable from the retrieved text | Not stated | Cloud/foundation-model inference; real-time benchmark simulated inference at 5 Hz; no Raspberry Pi/Jetson deployment reported | Real-world, multi-embodiment robot interactions | Exact trial count, precision, recall, false-success rate, image resolution, and a textual 82.4% result were not published in the retrieved passages; latency can make predictions stale (team2025geminirobotics1.5 pages 14-15) |
| Chemist Eye | 2026 | Peer-reviewed | PPE classification; dangerous-posture detection; robot decision success | Up to 97.5% PPE accuracy; 97% posture/hazard accuracy; 95% mean decision success | Query-specific denominators not stated; fire-response configurations used 10 trials each | Local LLaVA-7B and LLaVA-Phi3 models; specific Raspberry Pi/Jetson benchmark not reported | Self-driving-laboratory PPE, accident, and fire monitoring | Accuracy varied sharply with prompt (PPE: 67.5–97.5%); authors retained human judgment and did not consider it ready for autonomous safety decisions (munguiagaleano2026chemisteyea pages 6-7, munguiagaleano2026chemisteyea pages 1-2, munguiagaleano2026chemisteyea pages 5-6, munguiagaleano2026chemisteyea pages 7-8) |
| PREVENT | 2025 | Preprint | Deployed visual hazard/no-hazard accuracy; hazard-type accuracy | ResNet-18: 92.0–96.7%; fine-tuned ViT-L/14: 90.20–98.00% | Trial denominator not stated in the retrieved passage | Fine-tuned ResNet-18 and ViT-L/14; deployment platform not specified | Mobile robotic chemist: navigation, vial pickup, and vial placement | Misses involved small transparent obstacles, distant/partly visible vials, irregular textures, and combined spill/obstruction cases; no precision, recall, latency, or safety certification (veeramani2025preventproactiverisk pages 14-17) |


*Table: Comparison of published and preprint vision-based robot outcome and hazard detectors, emphasizing reported metrics, evaluation scale, edge-deployment evidence, and limitations. Missing precision, recall, false-success, or trial-count data are explicitly identified rather than inferred.*

**LIRA (Zhou et al. 2025; peer-reviewed).** The most directly relevant system for self-driving laboratories is LIRA, which uses a fine-tuned vision-language model on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin (64 GB) edge computing module. Across 200 manually introduced placement errors in two autonomous laboratory workflows (solid-state and synthesis), the fine-tuned VLM achieved 97.9% overall accuracy for determining whether placement was correct, 96.8% for classifying misalignment direction, and 98.9% for predicting whether an error was recoverable (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 5-7). Five failures occurred out of 200 tests (2 PXRD-plate and 3 NMR-rack errors), yielding a 97.5% error-inspection success rate (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 7-8, cooper2025liralocalizationinspection pages 9-10). By comparison, a conventional YOLOv11 classifier reached only 86.3%, and a zero-shot LLaVA-OneVision model achieved 42.9% (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 5-7). The system used an Intel RealSense D435i camera on the robot end effector and fixed webcams on instruments (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 8-9). DOI: 10.1038/s42004-025-01770-1.

**SuccessVQA / Flamingo (Du et al. 2023; preprint).** Fine-tuned Flamingo-3B evaluated on Panda gear-manipulation tasks achieved in-domain balanced accuracies of 82.1–96.0% for insertion and removal tasks, with approximately 50,000–60,000 episodes evaluated per task and 2,076 held-out episodes (du2023visionlanguagemodelsas pages 9-12). Critically, changing the viewpoint from the front basket camera (used for training) to the rear camera reduced balanced accuracy by up to 7.5 percentage points (from 96.0% to 89.7% for large-gear insertion; from 87.2% to 79.4% for large-gear removal) (du2023visionlanguagemodelsas pages 12-14). Adding distractor objects caused minimal degradation. This demonstrates that viewpoint is a significant factor even for fine-tuned models. arXiv: 2303.07280.

**Guardian (Pacaud et al. 2025; preprint).** Guardian-8B correctly recognized 91% of successful executions and 76% of failed executions, with a 9% false-positive rate on a UR5/RG6 multi-camera setup (pacaud2025guardiandetectingrobotic pages 9-11). On benchmark datasets, it achieved execution accuracy of 0.86 on RoboFail, 0.77 on UR5-Fail, and 0.85 on RoboVQA (pacaud2025guardiandetectingrobotic pages 5-6). arXiv: 2512.01946.

**Robometer (Liang et al. 2026; preprint).** On 100 Franka Panda DROID trajectories (30 successes, 70 failures, seven tasks), Robometer achieved a mean F1 of 0.81, outperforming RoboReward-4B (0.74), GPT-5-mini (0.33), and VLAC (0.16) (liang2026robometerscalinggeneralpurpose pages 9-10). arXiv: 2603.02115.

**Gemini Robotics-ER 1.5 (GR Team 2025; preprint).** The system was evaluated for binary video success detection across real-time (inference at 5 Hz) and offline settings, with both multiview and singleview inputs (team2025geminirobotics1.5 pages 14-15). The text emphasizes that stale predictions due to inference latency can render real-time judgments unreliable during dynamic interactions. The specific 82.4% figure mentioned in the user's context could not be confirmed from the retrieved text; Figure 13 of the paper plots values approximately ranging from the high-0.4s to about 0.8 depending on setting and model (team2025geminirobotics1.5 pages 14-15). arXiv: 2510.03342.

**FailBench (Navasardyan et al. 2026; preprint).** This cross-source benchmark evaluated 13 VLM-based detectors across 2,197 manipulation attempts from 14 independent sources (1,176 failures, 1,021 successes; 73% real-world). The strongest detector achieved 0.77 mean balanced accuracy. Critically, "no model exceeds 0.60 balanced accuracy on contact-rich assembly" (navasardyan2026failbenchhowreliable pages 2-4, navasardyan2026failbenchhowreliable pages 1-2). Purpose-built failure detectors generally underperformed general-purpose VLMs (navasardyan2026failbenchhowreliable pages 9-11). arXiv: 2609.03611.

**SAFE (Gu et al. 2025; preprint).** SAFE extracts VLA internal features and predicts failure likelihood. On real-world data, SAFE-MLP achieved ROC-AUC of 86.76–89.11 on seen tasks and 88.42 on unseen WidowX tasks (gu2026safemultitaskfailure pages 9-11). It uses functional conformal prediction to calibrate time-varying detection thresholds, with significance level α ≈ 0.15 providing a tradeoff between balanced accuracy and detection latency (gu2026safemultitaskfailure pages 19-21). arXiv: 2506.09937.

**Edge deployment.** Among the systems reviewed, only LIRA demonstrated deployment on edge hardware suitable for a small cloud lab (Jetson AGX Orin) (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 8-9, cooper2025liralocalizationinspection pages 10-13). No system reported deployment on a Raspberry Pi 5 for success/failure detection. The user's context mentions TOPReward; this system (arXiv: 2602.19313) uses token probabilities from VLMs as zero-shot rewards for robotics, evaluated on LeRobot datasets, but the retrieved text did not contain precision/recall metrics directly comparable to the other detectors.

---

### 2. Automatic Detection of Human Interventions and Presence

**Laboratory-specific systems.** Chemist Eye (Munguia-Galeano et al. 2026; peer-reviewed) achieved 97% accuracy for detecting potential safety hazards and 95% decision-making success in a self-driving laboratory with three mobile robots (munguiagaleano2026chemisteyea pages 1-2). For PPE compliance (lab coat detection), accuracy ranged from 67.5% to 97.5% depending on the prompt format, with LLaVA-Phi3 achieving the highest rates (munguiagaleano2026chemisteyea pages 5-6). Dangerous posture detection (lying, sitting, crawling) reached 97% accuracy (munguiagaleano2026chemisteyea pages 6-7). However, the authors explicitly stated the system was "not yet trustworthy for autonomous safety-related decisions" and retained human judgment as necessary (munguiagaleano2026chemisteyea pages 7-8). DOI: 10.1039/d6dd00062b.

PREVENT (Veeramani et al. 2025; preprint) used a fine-tuned ResNet-18 for visual hazard classification, achieving deployment accuracies of 92.0–96.7% across navigation, vial pickup, and vial placement tasks. A fine-tuned ViT-L/14 for hazard-type classification achieved 90.2–98.0% (veeramani2025preventproactiverisk pages 14-17). arXiv: 2510.21438.

**Edge hardware for hand/pose detection.** Ivačko et al. (2026; peer-reviewed) benchmarked a complete hand-tracking pipeline (MediaPipe Hands + Kalman smoothing + YOLO + LSTM) on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and a Raspberry Pi 5 with Hailo AI accelerator. End-to-end latency (frame acquisition to robot command) was approximately 160 ms on the Jetson and 280 ms on the Raspberry Pi (ivacko2026edgecomputingapproach pages 22-24), corresponding to approximately 6 FPS and 3.5 FPS respectively. DOI: 10.3390/computers15040241.

**Camera-based safety under ISO standards.** Under ISO 10218, when the distance between a robot and a person falls below a defined safety level, the robot must slow down and stop (ozkahraman2021designandvalidation pages 1-2). Camera-based safety systems have achieved response times of 0.08–0.1 seconds and can operate at a minimum illuminance of 120 lux (versus 400 lux for commercial systems), with at least 1080p resolution recommended (ozkahraman2021designandvalidation pages 15-18). DOI: 10.3390/app112411679.

However, **no published camera-based safety system using deep learning has demonstrated certification to ISO 13849 Performance Level d or e, or compliance with IEC 61496 as electro-sensitive protective equipment.** The retrieved literature discusses these standards in context but does not present a system that has achieved formal safety certification for camera-based human detection (ozkahraman2021designandvalidation pages 13-15, ozkahraman2021designandvalidation pages 18-20). Camera-based intrusion detection for robot safety remains a research topic rather than a certified solution. For safety-critical functions, commercial systems (e.g., Pilz SafetyEye using three cameras with a certified safety controller) provide certified solutions, but research literature on their internal detection accuracy and false-alarm rates is sparse (lettera2024amultimodalworkspace pages 54-59). ISO 10218:2025 (the latest revision) may address camera-based monitoring more explicitly, but the retrieved sources primarily reference the 2011 edition.

**Implication for the BYU Vertical Cloud Lab.** Camera-based hand detection can serve for logging human interventions (a non-safety-critical function) with sub-300 ms latency on a Raspberry Pi 5 with accelerator. For safety-rated stopping, a separate certified system would be required under current standards.

---

### 3. Camera Verification of Placement and Insertion for Labware

LIRA provides the most detailed published evidence. The fine-tuned VLM classified placement correctness at 97.9%, misalignment direction at 96.8%, and recoverability at 98.9% across 200 tests involving Chemspeed vial racks, PXRD plates, NMR racks, and LCMS racks (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 5-7). In a separate evaluation, 600 vial pickup-and-insertion manipulations achieved 100% success rate (cooper2025liralocalizationinspection pages 6-9). The system used a wrist-mounted RealSense D435i camera on a KUKA KMR iiwa for post-placement inspection (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 8-9). Failures were attributed to "visually ambiguous conditions, such as similar rack/holder colors or cluttered backgrounds" (cooper2025liralocalizationinspection pages 9-10). DOI: 10.1038/s42004-025-01770-1.

**Smallest detectable offsets.** No published work was found that specifically quantifies the smallest positional offset (in mm) detectable by a vision system for labware placement verification. LIRA's misalignment classification distinguishes translational offsets (left, right, forward, backward) from rotational errors, treating translational errors as recoverable and rotational errors as requiring human intervention (cooper2025liralocalizationinspection pages 6-9), but it does not report minimum detectable displacement thresholds. **This remains a gap in the published literature** relevant to the user's vial-seating and stub-insertion verification needs.

**Fontenot et al. 2026** was not found in the literature search. No publication matching this author and date was retrievable. If it exists, it may be too recent to have been indexed.

---

### 4. Calibration Maintenance and Drift Detection

**AnchorHEC (Hwang et al. 2026; preprint)** is a targetless hand-eye calibration framework for jointly calibrating wrist and fixed cameras using RGB images, forward kinematics, and known camera intrinsics, without calibration targets. On a physical robot, wrist-camera calibration achieved 1.22–1.35 cm translation error and 1.00–1.48° rotation error at 15 wrist poses (hwang2026anchorhectargetlesshandeye pages 5-6, hwang2026anchorhectargetlesshandeye pages 7-8). Fixed-camera translation errors averaged approximately 1.29 cm for accepted registrations (hwang2026anchorhectargetlesshandeye pages 7-8). The method supports recalibration from a single scene acquisition without dedicated targets. arXiv: 2611.02884.

**Self-calibration using contact.** Limoyo et al. (2018; peer-reviewed) demonstrated targetless self-calibration for mobile manipulators using point-cloud registration, achieving centimeter-level accuracy for end-effector positioning under visual guidance. DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.1803.06406.

**Drift detection.** No published work was found that specifically addresses automated detection of extrinsic calibration drift during long campaigns. The standard approach in robotics is periodic re-verification against known fiducial markers—which aligns with the user's current AprilTag infrastructure. A practical self-check would compare the detected tag poses against their known fixture positions at regular intervals; if reprojection error exceeds a threshold, recalibration is triggered. **No published study reports how often recalibration is needed for low-cost cameras like the IMX477**, nor whether the IMX477 exhibits greater thermal or mechanical drift than industrial cameras. This is an open gap.

---

### 5. Measuring and Bounding False-Clear / False-Success Rates for Vision Gates

**Conformal prediction** provides the most principled framework for bounding false-negative rates (missed failures) of vision-based decision gates. Luo et al. (2023; peer-reviewed) demonstrated that conformal prediction can tune warning systems to provably achieve a false-negative rate ≤ ε using as few as 1/ε unsafe calibration examples—approximately 20 examples for a 5% FNR target (luo2024sampleefficientsafetyassurances pages 8-9, luo2024sampleefficientsafetyassurances pages 7-8, luo2024sampleefficientsafetyassurances pages 1-2). The key tradeoff is that demanding very low FNR imposes a lower bound on false-positive rate: FPR ≥ 1 − (1+T)·ε, where T is the training-set size (luo2024sampleefficientsafetyassurances pages 8-9). DOI: 10.1177/02783649231221580.

**PAC-Bayes bounds.** Farid et al. (2022; preprint) achieved misclassification bounds of 0.128 for standard navigation and 0.154 for occluded-obstacle settings using PAC-Bayes analysis of a vision-based failure predictor. In 15 physical trials per setting, no false negatives (collisions) occurred when the predictor was used (farid2202failurepredictionwith pages 7-8). arXiv: 2202.05894.

**SAFE's functional conformal prediction.** SAFE uses a time-varying conformal prediction band calibrated on successful rollouts, with significance level α (typically 0.15) controlling the accuracy-latency tradeoff. A failure is flagged when the score exceeds the threshold (gu2026safemultitaskfailure pages 4-6, gu2026safemultitaskfailure pages 19-21). This framework is directly applicable to gating decisions like "is the plate clear?"

**Practical implication for the plate-clear check.** No published study reports the false-clear rate of a specific vision gate for 3D-printer plate clearing. To measure this, one would: (a) collect labeled examples of clear and not-clear plates, (b) run the classifier on a held-out set, (c) apply conformal prediction to bound the false-clear (false-negative) rate at a user-specified level (e.g., ε = 0.05), requiring approximately 20 deliberately not-clear images. The conformal guarantee holds marginally under exchangeability; distribution shifts (lighting changes, camera drift) can violate this assumption.

---

### 6. Privacy, Governance, and Anonymization Effects

**Effect of face blurring on downstream detection.** Ren et al. (2018; peer-reviewed) found that Gaussian face blurring reduced spatial action detection mAP on the DALY dataset from 56.85% to 42.39–51.97% depending on blur severity (a 5–14.5 point drop), while masking caused the largest degradation to 38.86% (ren2018learningtoanonymize pages 9-11). Their adversarially learned anonymizer maintained mAP at 52.32%, outperforming all hand-crafted methods. arXiv: 1803.11556.

Lee & You (2024; peer-reviewed) found that face blurring reduced YOLOv8x bbox mAP by 2.6 points and RT-DETR-L by 7.5 points on COCO, but person-class detection was relatively robust due to the strong representation of persons in training data (lee2024balancingprivacyand pages 8-10). DOI: 10.1109/ACCESS.2024.3352146.

Abdulaziz & Bondarev (2026; peer-reviewed) showed that for video anomaly detection, blurring caused only minor AUC degradation (0.2–0.5 points for robust models like UR-DMU and PEL4VAD), while masking could paradoxically improve some models but at the cost of extreme false-alarm rates (99.65% for BN-WVAD) (abdulaziz2026unmaskingperformancegaps pages 6-9, abdulaziz2026unmaskingperformancegaps pages 9-13). DOI: 10.1007/978-3-032-07343-3_14.

**Practical guidance for the BYU lab.** At 720p and 5 FPS with on-device face blurring, the user's setup should expect modest degradation (2–8 points mAP) for person and object detection. For hand-entry detection, hands are typically not blurred, so hand-detection accuracy should be unaffected by face anonymization. Activity recognition for face-centric actions (e.g., drinking) would be more impacted, but laboratory manipulations are hand-centric and thus less sensitive.

**Governance.** No published standard specific to laboratory video governance was found. General guidance from GDPR and institutional review board frameworks applies: face de-identification should occur at the point of capture (as the user is already doing), retention policies should be defined and enforced, and access controls should limit who can view raw (un-blurred) footage. The key unresolved question is whether blurred video constitutes personal data under applicable regulations if re-identification is technically possible through de-blurring attacks, as noted in the privacy literature (abdulaziz2026unmaskingperformancegaps pages 1-3).

---

### Summary of Gaps in Published Evidence

Several aspects of the user's question have **no published evidence**:

1. **False-clear rate of a 3D-printer plate check**: No study has measured this specific vision gate's error rate.
2. **Smallest detectable labware offset** (in mm): Not quantified in any retrieved publication.
3. **Calibration drift rates for IMX477 or similar low-cost cameras**: No published data.
4. **How often recalibration is needed** for wrist or fixed cameras during long laboratory campaigns: Not reported.
5. **ISO 13849/IEC 61496 certification of camera-based detection**: No deep-learning camera system has achieved formal safety certification for robot workcell human detection.
6. **Laboratory-specific video retention or governance standards**: None found; general data-protection frameworks apply.
7. **Fontenot et al. 2026**: Not found in the literature search.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides aggregate FailBench results rather than precision, recall, false-success rate, or model-by-model trial counts. FailBench contains 2,197 manipulation attempts from 14 public sources: 12 real-world and 2 simulated datasets. It evaluates 13 VLM-based failure detectors. The strongest detector achieves 0.77 mean balanced accuracy, indicating that current systems remain unreliable when transferred beyond their original evaluation settings. Performance depends more on the visual evidence needed to determine success than on the robot or task domain. Detection is comparatively strong when success can be inferred from observable object motion, but approaches chance when determining success requires establishing physical contact; no model exceeds 0.60 balanced accuracy on contact-intensive assembly tasks. Models fine-tuned specifically for robot failure detection generally underperform general-purpose VLMs and their corresponding pretrained models. A visual-input intervention that crops the outcome-relevant region improves the strongest detector by 2.4 percentage points without additional training. The excerpt does not report numerical results for LIRA, Gemini Robotics ER, Robometer, TOPReward, AHA, Guardian, SuccessVQA, or SAFE, nor does it provide FailBench precision, recall, false-success rate, or per-detector trial counts.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides quantitative results only for FailBench, not for LIRA, Gemini Robotics ER, Robometer, TOPReward, AHA, Guardian, SuccessVQA, or SAFE. FailBench evaluates vision-language models for judging robot manipulation success across 2,197 attempts drawn from fourteen public sources. Among thirteen tested detectors, the strongest achieves 0.77 mean balanced accuracy. The excerpt does not report separate precision, recall, false-success rate, or trial counts for individual detectors, nor does it provide a breakdown of FailBench’s 2,197 attempts by detector or source. Qualitatively, purpose-built failure detectors underperform general-purpose VLMs, and fine-tuning for failure detection may reduce performance outside the training data. Performance is substantially better when success is visible through coarse object motion, but approaches chance when correct judgment requires fine-grained physical contact reasoning. Cropping the outcome-relevant region improves the strongest detector by 2.3 points without retraining, although the effect varies by source and does not resolve contact-level failures. The conclusion frames reliable robot failure detection as an open problem and warns that evaluations conducted only on a model’s development source can overstate reliability.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides information only about Gemini Robotics-ER 1.5 (GR-ER 1.5) and related baseline models on real-world robot-interaction success detection. The task is framed as predicting a binary success/failure signal from images plus a textual task instruction. Results are divided into four settings: real-time multiview, real-time singleview, offline multiview, and offline singleview success detection. Real-time evaluation uses recorded real-world robot rollouts, runs inference at 5 Hz, and accounts for latency by assigning each frame the most recent available prediction; the text emphasizes that stale predictions can become irrelevant during dynamic interactions. Offline evaluation permits unlimited inference time and uses videos spanning different embodiments, viewpoints, and input formats. Figure 13 reports accuracy comparisons among Gemini Robotics-ER 1.5, Gemini Robotics-ER, Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash, GPT-5, and GPT-5-mini, with plotted values approximately ranging from the high 0.4s to around 0.8 depending on the setting and model. It provides only broader FailBench findings and a few comparison figures. FailBench evaluates 13 failure detectors across 14 independently collected sources and 2,197 robot execution attempts, covering policy rollouts, human teleoperation, and constructed failures with single- and multi-view observations. Detector performance varies substantially with the evidence needed: models are more reliable when success is determined by which object moved, but approach chance when success depends on establishing physical contact; no model exceeds 0.60 balanced accuracy on contact-rich assembly. General-purpose models outperform the specialists discussed, while all five directly comparable fine-tuned specialists perform worse than their base models. An evidence-localization crop improves the strongest detector’s mean balanced accuracy by 2.3 points without retraining. The excerpt also cites 0.89 balanced accuracy for GPT-4o on WorldGym’s RT-1 labels and 67% zero-shot transfer for PRIMO R1 to RoboFail, but these are not the requested detector-by-detector precision/recall/error-rate results. It notes that prior evaluations were generally single-source, whereas FailBench uses a cross-source protocol.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that LIRA achieved a 97.5% error-inspection success rate, described as its reliability in detecting and addressing task-level failures. It was evaluated in two autonomous self-driving-laboratory workflows: a solid-state workflow and a synthesis workflow. In the solid-state workflow, LIRA reduced manipulation time by 34%; in the synthesis workflow, it enabled remote inspection for a robot. The system used an edge-computing device to perform real-time image processing and run the fine-tuned vision-language model. The architecture included a robot client interface, a communication layer, and an edge-device server, with ArUco-based localization and a VLM inspection node. contexts.context: The excerpt reports that the fine-tuned LIRA inspection model achieved 97.9% overall accuracy. Its task-specific accuracies were 97.9% for determining whether placement was correct, 96.8% for classifying misalignment direction, and 98.9% for predicting whether an error was recoverable. For comparison, the conventional YOLOv11 classifier reached 86.3%, while the untuned zero-shot LLaVA-OneVision model achieved 42.9% overall success, with 77.7% placement, 25.5% direction, and 25.5% recoverability accuracy. The passage indicates that 200 evaluations were conducted across the solid-state and synthesis workflows, although the excerpt ends before clarifying whether this count refers to images, trials, or errors specifically. Evaluated tasks included rack and plate placement-offset inspection, misalignment-direction classification, error-recoverability reasoning, PXRD door-state inspection, and rack-placement inspection at Chemspeed, LCMS, and NMR stations. The system used a KUKA KMR iiwa mobile manipulator, a RealSense D435i camera on the robot end effector for post-placement inspection and localization, fixed webcams on laboratory instruments for remote inspection, and a Jetson AGX Orin edge computer receiving images wirelessly. Recoverability was not evaluated for LCMS and NMR racks because their constrained placement spaces made robotic correction impractical.

contexts.context: AnchorHEC is a targetless hand-eye calibration method for jointly calibrating a robot wrist camera and fixed cameras, without calibration targets. The approach uses reconstructed wrist-camera poses and forward-kinematics information, with FK-selected image pairs, confidence-based weighting, and a robust objective for the initial estimate. For fixed cameras, it pools reconstructed 2D–3D correspondences, estimates camera poses using RANSAC PnP and nonlinear refinement, and applies an ambiguity rejection rule; unsupported or rejected registrations fall back to a corrected shared-reconstruction-frame pose. Experiments used DUSt3R, MASt3R, VGGT, and ViPE reconstructions, with five trials, 15 wrist poses, and five fixed-camera frames unless otherwise stated. The excerpt reports translation error et and geodesic rotation error eθ, though their units are not shown in the supplied text. With the default VGGT backbone and 15 wrist poses, AnchorHEC (“Ours”) obtained wrist-camera errors of et=2.98 and eθ=0.41 in the room scene, and et=1.02 and eθ=0.22 on the tabletop. For fixed cameras, the corresponding errors were et=1.79 and eθ=0.32 in the room, and et=0.66 and eθ=0.19 on the tabletop. With 25 wrist poses, the reported errors improved further: wrist room 0.79/0.20, wrist tabletop 0.16/0.09, fixed room 1.40/0.29, and fixed tabletop 0.55/0.18.

contexts.context: AnchorHEC is the paper’s targetless hand-eye calibration method for jointly calibrating a robot wrist camera and one or more fixed cameras without a calibration target. The excerpt describes a 3DFM-based pipeline with FK-guided image-pair selection and an exact-FK objective, evaluated in simulation and on a physical robot. In simulation, AnchorHEC’s mean wrist translation and rotation errors were lower than JCR’s by 84.6% and 70.0%, respectively, averaged over 24 backbone/scene/pose-budget conditions. For four jointly reconstructed fixed cameras, the reported AnchorHEC errors were 1.78 cm/0.27° in room scenes and 1.43 cm/0.29° in tabletop scenes. With no fixed cameras (wrist-only), the corresponding errors were 1.06 cm/0.22° for room scenes and 0.21 cm/0.11° for tabletop scenes; values remained approximately 1.02 cm/0.22° and 0.19 cm/0.10° for most mixed-camera settings. In the physical-robot evaluation at Nw=5, AnchorHEC achieved 3.50 cm/1.62° for room wrist-camera calibration and 6.10 cm/2.37° for tabletop; at Nw=15, it achieved 1.35 cm/1.48° and 1.22 cm/1.11°, respectively. Translation errors are centimeters and rotation errors are degrees.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes AnchorHEC as a targetless, scene-based framework that calibrates wrist-mounted and fixed cameras together in one procedure. It uses RGB images of a shared scene, forward-kinematics (FK) poses, known camera intrinsics, and a 3D reconstruction framework. Its stages include shared reconstruction-frame initialization, kinematics-anchored wrist-camera refinement, and fixed-camera registration. Wrist-camera estimation uses relative reconstructed motions, FK-guided selection of motion pairs with diverse rotation axes, and bundle adjustment; fixed cameras are registered to metric scene geometry anchored by the refined wrist transform and FK. Dense image matching is used to establish wrist/fixed-camera correspondences, with reconstruction-based estimates as a fallback. The excerpt states that the method was validated in simulation across reconstruction backbones and evaluated on a physical robot, but it does not provide the achieved calibration accuracy or numerical translation and rotation errors. Those results would need to be obtained from later experimental/results sections of the paper.

snippets: A scene-based framework for targetless calibration of wrist and fixed cameras in a single procedure from RGB images of a common scene, FK, and known intrinsics.
Kinematics-anchored wrist-camera estimation combining FK-guided pair selection with image-based refinement to reduce the impact of reconstruction errors.

contexts.context: AnchorHEC is a targetless hand-eye calibration framework designed to calibrate both wrist-mounted (eye-in-hand) and fixed (eye-to-hand) cameras in one procedure. It uses RGB images, forward-kinematics poses, and known camera intrinsics, initializing both camera types through a shared 3D foundation-model reconstruction. The method refines the wrist-camera transform with FK-constrained bundle adjustment, then uses the refined wrist transform and FK to triangulate metric scene points and register the fixed-camera poses. The excerpt reports relative calibration improvements rather than absolute translation or rotation error values: across three reconstruction backbones and averaged over both wrist and fixed cameras, AnchorHEC reduced translation calibration error by 86.4% and rotation calibration error by 71.6% compared with reconstruction-based baselines. It was also validated on a physical robot. No absolute numerical translation or rotation errors are provided in the supplied excerpt.

contexts.context: AnchorHEC is presented as a targetless, single-scene calibration procedure for both wrist-mounted and fixed cameras. It refines the wrist transform, uses forward kinematics (FK) to triangulate metric scene points, and then estimates fixed-camera poses through matching, triangulation, PnP, registration, and an ambiguity test. The excerpt reports several accuracy measures rather than one universal number. Across mixed-camera runs, mean fixed-camera translation error decreased from 7.28 cm initially to 5.42 cm after wrist-camera refinement, scale refitting, and axial correction, and finally to 2.61 cm after registration and ambiguity testing. Accepted registrations averaged 1.29 cm translation error; rejected cases used fallback estimates averaging 16.51 cm. For the physical tabletop acquisition, the full pipeline reduced mean wrist translation error from 1.48 cm to 1.22 cm. The displayed “Ours” results include wrist translation/rotation pairs such as 1.02 cm/0.22° and 0.19 cm/0.10°, and another physical setting reports 1.35 cm/1.48° and 1.22 cm/1.11°. Dense matching produced 1.58 cm mean final fixed-camera translation error, compared with 4.51 cm for SIFT. Thus, the excerpt supports approximately 1.22–1.35 cm wrist translation accuracy in physical tests and 2.61 cm overall fixed-camera translation accuracy, with rotation errors in the displayed results ranging from 0.10° to 1.48° depending on setting.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes an experimental, camera-based safety system for fenceless robot workcells, but it does not specify the requirements of ISO 13849, IEC 61496, or ISO 10218 in terms of safety categories, Safety Integrity Level (SIL), Performance Level (PL), diagnostic coverage, fault tolerance, or validation procedures. The experiments used two 2-D cameras and a ResNet-152 deep-learning classifier, with image merging intended to reduce blind spots. The reported design target was at least 1080p resolution at 23 frames per second; camera resolution significantly affected response time, whereas graphics-processor performance did not significantly affect it. The system operated at a minimum illuminance of 120 lux and showed similar performance when scaled to a larger robot workcell. contexts.context: The excerpt does not specify the detailed requirements of ISO 13849, IEC 61496, or ISO 10218, nor does it state a required Safety Integrity Level (SIL), Performance Level (PL), response-time limit, or numerical detection-accuracy target. It describes a camera-based safety concept in which image processing detects movement by comparing sequential image histograms and sends deceleration or stop commands to the robot controller. The model treats minimum detectable object size, camera lens angle, camera height, resolution, pixel count, and safety distance as important design variables. At least two symmetrically positioned cameras are recommended to prevent blind areas caused by the robot arm. The proposed partial image-masking and stitching method combines non-overlapping image regions to avoid blind spots and reduce duplicate processing. contexts.context: The excerpt does not directly report face-blurring effects on generic activity recognition, action detection, or human-detection accuracy; it evaluates video anomaly detection (VAD) under human-region anonymization. For the reported VAD AUC results, blurring (HB) causes only a small degradation: UR-DMU falls from 85.85% on raw video to 85.63%, a 0.25% relative drop, while PEL4VAD falls from 85.16% to 84.72%, a 0.51% drop. Human masking (HM) produces slightly larger reductions: UR-DMU reaches 85.08% (0.89% drop), and PEL4VAD reaches 84.53% (0.74% drop). Qualitatively, blurring and encryption generate larger frame-level score fluctuations and more false alarms in normal events. Encryption is especially damaging for the Assault, Shoplifting, and Vandalism categories because it distorts spatial and temporal information and creates non-smooth transitions. Masking can sometimes appear to improve certain models or classes, but the excerpt attributes these gains to sensitivity to anonymization noise rather than genuine recognition improvement. Overall, UR-DMU and PEL4VAD are relatively robust, whereas effects vary substantially by model, anonymization method, and activity class.

contexts.context: The excerpt shows that face anonymization generally improves privacy by increasing face-verification error, but reduces activity/action recognition accuracy. On both the DALY and JHMDB datasets, conventional methods such as blurring, masking, adding noise, edge replacement, and super-pixel processing harmed action detection relative to un-anonymized video. DALY frame-mAP for un-anonymized frames was 56.85%. Blur reduced it to 42.39% with 8x8 downsampling (a 14.46-point drop), 48.10% with 16x16 (8.75 points), and 51.97% with 24x24 (4.88 points). Noise achieved 49.91%, 46.47%, and 43.81% for increasing variance levels, corresponding to drops of 6.94, 10.38, and 13.04 points. Edge and super-pixel processing yielded 47.99% and 46.92%, respectively. The proposed method achieved 52.32% mAP, outperforming all anonymization baselines while remaining near the un-anonymized result. It especially improved actions involving the face, such as drinking, phoning, playing harmonica, and taking photos. Its anonymizer modifies face pixels, while an activity-detection model encourages changes that maintain or maximize activity-detection performance. contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that face anonymization creates a privacy–recognition trade-off. Conventional methods illustrated in the figure—8×8 blurring, masking, Gaussian noise, super-pixels, and edge-based modification—can conceal identity, but they may reduce action-detection accuracy, particularly when the action depends on visual information around the face, head, or mouth. The cited examples include playing harmonica, brushing teeth, phoning, and applying make-up. The method described in the paper uses adversarial face modification to make identity unrecognizable while retaining pose, brightness, scene structure, and action information through an L1 photorealistic loss. Its detector is trained jointly with the face modifier, and the modifier is later fixed while the action detector is fine-tuned to stabilize optimization. The excerpt does not report numerical accuracy values or percentage performance degradation for blurring, masking, noise, super-pixel, edge, or the proposed anonymization method. It also does not provide separate human-detection accuracy results; it describes spatial action detection using Faster R-CNN and evaluates action detection with mAP at IoU 0.5. Thus, the qualitative conclusion is that stronger or poorly designed face concealment can impair activity/action recognition, especially for face-centered actions, while the proposed approach is designed to reduce that degradation.

Conventional approaches—including blurring, pixelation, encryption, masking, and avatar replacement—are described as potentially degrading utility. For the study’s main video-anomaly-detection experiments, anonymized data remain usable, and performance is algorithm-dependent. It also does not report comparative degradation figures for each anonymization method within the supplied pages. It does establish the broader trade-off: stronger privacy protection and concealment of human identity may reduce visual utility and scene quality, while privacy-by-design methods can preserve utility but may limit visual monitoring and flexibility with generic image-processing algorithms.

It reports results for four human-anonymization techniques that mask, distort, or replace sensitive body regions in video anomaly detection. The overall finding is that anonymization does not automatically cause a performance collapse: its effect varies substantially by model and anonymization method. In some cases, anonymization artifacts can even improve anomaly-detection performance—for example, MGFN with encryption and BN-WVAD with masking. For models using I3D features, performance under anonymization depends strongly on architecture and learning strategy. The excerpt also contrasts conventional anonymization with privacy-by-design approaches: conventional methods generally retain scene context and therefore offer greater flexibility for downstream tasks, while privacy-by-design methods optimize a narrower utility and may compromise performance. contexts.context: The excerpt evaluates anonymization effects on object detection and instance segmentation, rather than activity recognition or action detection specifically. For human/person detection, the reported performance change is relatively minor, which the authors associate with the strong representation of the person class in COCO (58.7% of the training data), compared with vehicle classes (4.5%). In contrast, motorcycle, bus, and truck recognition declines substantially. Across anonymization methods, overall degradation is described as similar, but distortion and mask-out produce more pronounced declines because they remove or obscure larger amounts of visual information. Blurring and pixelation preserve more information and therefore generally have less impact. The architecture also matters: on the COCO validation set, YOLOv8x suffered bbox mAP declines of 2.6 points with blurring, 2.4 with pixelation, 3.1 with distortion, and 2.5 with mask-out. RT-DETR-L declines were substantially larger: 7.5, 4.6, 5.8, and 5.4 points, respectively. For bbox mAP50, YOLO declines were 3.4, 3.4, 4.0, and 3.4 points, while RT-DETR declines were 7.7, 5.6, 7.0, and 6.3 points. Thus, the excerpt supports conclusions about detection accuracy, especially person detection, but does not provide direct measurements for activity-recognition or action-detection accuracy.
contexts.question: What is the effect of face blurring and anonymization on activity recognition, action detection, and human detection accuracy? How much does performance degrade with different anonymization methods?

contexts.context: The excerpt presents theoretical results relevant to vision-based failure prediction and safety gating, together with an empirical driver-alert validation. For warning rules based only on the ranking of surrogate safety scores, if the rule issues no warning for at least one possible input, the false-negative rate (FNR) and false-positive rate (FPR) obey FNR ≥ γ/(1+T) and FPR ≥ 1−γ, implying the tradeoff FPR ≥ 1−(1+T)FNR. Thus, demanding a very small FNR necessarily imposes a lower bound on FPR unless the warning rule is nearly always active. Under exchangeability, conformal learning provides a marginal false-negative guarantee for every test point, whereas PAC learning requires i.i.d. data and gives its guarantee only with probability 1−δ. The reported sample complexity is Θ(1/ϵ) unsafe training examples for conformal learning, compared with Θ(1/ϵ²) for standard PAC analysis. The excerpt does not state a numerical experiment-specific sample count or measured FPR/FNR; it says the driver-alert experiments verified the Proposition 1 FNR bound while maintaining low FPR. It also notes that verifying even a fixed warning function by concentration can require Θ(1/ϵ²) samples.
contexts.question: What specific results did conformal prediction achieve for bounding false positive and false negative rates in robot vision-based failure prediction and safety gating? What sample sizes were needed?

contexts.context: The excerpt provides theoretical rather than application-specific numerical results for conformal prediction in safety gating. Algorithm 1 guarantees a false-negative/safety-violation rate of at most ϵ + 1/(1+|A|), where |A| is the number of unsafe calibration examples. To attain a target safety level ϵ*, the algorithm selects ϵ so that ϵ + 1/(1+|A|) ≤ ϵ*. The term 1/(1+|A|) is the discretization error. Increasing ϵ lowers the false-positive rate because the system issues fewer warnings, so the largest admissible ϵ is preferred. The excerpt also states a lower bound showing that no ϵ-safe warning system based only on the ordering of surrogate scores can achieve an FPR below 1−(1+T)ϵ, where T is the training-set size; thus very stringent safety levels can force many false alarms. A nontrivial positive ϵ requires |A| > 1/ϵ*−1; otherwise the method always warns. In practice, about |A| ≈ 1.5/ϵ*−1 unsafe examples was reported as sufficient, with roughly 30 unsafe examples cited for a 5% FPR. The excerpt does not give separate empirical rates or sample sizes specifically for a robot vision-based failure-prediction experiment.
